+// This does mean that `int64_t` and `struct { int64_t }` have different calling conventions but this behaviour matches the base integer calling convention.
+
+* For aggregates that can be passed in pairs of registers,   they are never split into one register part and one on-stack part.
+  Instead of splitting the entire aggregate is passed on the stack.
+* Aggregates larger than `2*YLEN` or with an alignment larger than the stack alignment are always passed by reference.
+* All other aggregates follow the base calling convention.
+* Unions follow the same rules as aggregates: if they are `YLEN`-bit aligned and less than or equal to `2*YLEN` bits in size,   they are passed in memory layout in `YLEN` registers.
+  Otherwise, the base calling convention rules apply.
+
+==== Variadic and On-Stack Arguments
+
+In the pure-capability ABIs, variadic and on-stack arguments are handled differently from the base integer calling convention to ensure capability safety and allow for bounded `va_list` implementations.
+
+1. All variadic arguments (those corresponding to the `...` in the function prototype) are passed on the stack.
+They never occupy argument registers `a0`-`a7`.
+Each variadic argument is passed in a `YLEN`-aligned stack slot.
++
+NOTE: Passing all variadic arguments on the stack simplifies the implementation of `va_list` and ensures capability safety.
+Measurements on other architectures (AArch64) have shown that most variadic functions are simply wrappers around a function taking a `va_list`.
+In standard ABIs that pass variadic arguments in registers, the callee must spill these registers to the stack to create a contiguous `va_list` structure, which adds overhead and complicates the implementation.
+Passing all variadic arguments on the stack from the start simplifies these wrappers and avoids complex register-to-stack spilling logic.
+Using `YLEN`-sized slots for all arguments, including those smaller than `YLEN`, further avoids the need for complex logic to determine the offset of each argument.
+This approach has been used successfully in other CHERI-enabled architectures such as Morello and was also adopted by Apple in the variadic calling convention for AArch64 on iOS and macOS.
+
+2. A capability that covers all on-stack arguments on the stack is passed in the `x5` (`t0`) register.
+3. For variadic functions, this capability has its `Store` and `Execute` permissions cleared.
+4. If no on-stack arguments are passed to a variadic function, the `x5` register is set to null.

 that require load and store alignments of more than 32 bits. In particular, this
 calling convention must not be used with the D ISA extension.
 
+[[cheri-cc]]
+=== RVY Pure-Capability Calling Conventions
+
+IMPORTANT: RVY Pure-Capability ABIs are experimental.
+
+These calling conventions are used when the base ISA is RVY and a pure-capability ABI is in use.
+In these ABIs, all pointers (including the stack pointer, frame pointer, and return address) are represented as capabilities (using the extended GPRs).
+
+The register names and usage remain the same as the <<integer-cc,integer calling convention>>, but the registers `x0`-`x31` (and their ABI aliases) now refer to the `YLEN`-wide extended GPRs.
+Any integer operation (e.g., add/multiply/etc.) writing to the `x1`-`x31` registers sets the address bits and clears the metadata.
+
+The pure-capability ABIs closely follow the same calling conventions as the base integer and hardware floating-point calling conventions, but since the GPRs are now `YLEN` bits wide the following differences exist:
+
+* Variadic and on-stack arguments use a different register convention (see next subsection).
+* `2*XLEN` (i.e. `YLEN`) wide scalars are passed in a single argument register if they are of pointer type (including `(u)intptr_t`).
++
+NOTE: For non-pointer scalar types the maximum size passed in a single argument register is still `XLEN` rather than `YLEN`.
+This avoids the implementation difficulty of passing `int64_t` in a single register when `YLEN` is 64 (RV32).
+// It also reflects that the high bits of capability registers cannot be used for computation directly as they need to be copied to another register using `YHIR` first.
+// A future calling convention variant may allow for packing these types in a single register.
+
+* Aggregates up to `2*YLEN` bits are passed in `YLEN` argument register(s) (using the memory layout of the aggregate) if they are at least `YLEN`-bit aligned.
++
+NOTE: This rule is required to ensure that aggregates that could potentially be used to store capabilities, but do not declare capability members (such as `alignas(16) char bytes[16]`) are passed in capability registers instead of being split into two registers (which would invalidate the capability tag).
+// This does mean that `int64_t` and `struct { int64_t }` have different calling conventions but this behaviour matches the base integer calling convention.
body:
On the implementation challenges front, we have implementation experience doing f64 in YLEN GPRs on CHERIoT. This causes modeling challenges for the LLVM backend, as you end up with a type that is legal (as in can be stored in a register), but on which almost no operations are legal. This was workable for an FP type, but required a lot of whackamoling of issues.

I expect doing the same for an integer type to be 
much more challenging, as LLVM bakes in a lot more assumptions of what operations should be legal on a legal integer type.

This is maybe not a disqualifying concern (it's ultimately software and can probably be worked around _somehow_), but in combination with the fact that we believe overall code quality will be better with split i64/i128, it seems clear to us that splitting is the correct choice.

diff_hunk:
@@ -675,6 +683,72 @@ The ILP32E calling convention is not compatible with ISAs that have registers
 that require load and store alignments of more than 32 bits. In particular, this
 calling convention must not be used with the D ISA extension.
 
+[[cheri-cc]]
+=== RVY Pure-Capability Calling Conventions
+
+IMPORTANT: RVY Pure-Capability ABIs are experimental.
+
+These calling conventions are used when the base ISA is RVY and a pure-capability ABI is in use.
+In these ABIs, all pointers (including the stack pointer, frame pointer, and return address) are represented as capabilities (using the extended GPRs).
+
+The register names and usage remain the same as the <<integer-cc,integer calling convention>>, but the registers `x0`-`x31` (and their ABI aliases) now refer to the `YLEN`-wide extended GPRs.
+Any integer operation (e.g., add/multiply/etc.) writing to the `x1`-`x31` registers sets the address bits and clears the metadata.
+
+The pure-capability ABIs closely follow the same calling conventions as the base integer and hardware floating-point calling conventions, but since the GPRs are now `YLEN` bits wide the following differences exist:
+
+* Variadic and on-stack arguments use a different register convention (see next subsection).
+* `2*XLEN` (i.e. `YLEN`) wide scalars are passed in a single argument register if they are of pointer type (including `(u)intptr_t`).
++
+NOTE: For non-pointer scalar types the maximum size passed in a single argument register is still `XLEN` rather than `YLEN`.
+This avoids the implementation difficulty of passing `int64_t` in a single register when `YLEN` is 64 (RV32).
+// It also reflects that the high bits of capability registers cannot be used for computation directly as they need to be copied to another register using `YHIR` first.
+// A future calling convention variant may allow for packing these types in a single register.
+
+* Aggregates up to `2*YLEN` bits are passed in `YLEN` argument register(s) (using the memory layout of the aggregate) if they are at least `YLEN`-bit aligned.
++
+NOTE: This rule is required to ensure that aggregates that could potentially be used to store capabilities, but do not declare capability members (such as `alignas(16) char bytes[16]`) are passed in capability registers instead of being split into two registers (which would invalidate the capability tag).
+// This does mean that `int64_t` and `struct { int64_t }` have different calling conventions but this behaviour matches the base integer calling convention.
+
+* For aggregates that can be passed in pairs of registers,   they are never split into one register part and one on-stack part.
+  Instead of splitting the entire aggregate is passed on the stack.
+* Aggregates larger than `2*YLEN` or with an alignment larger than the stack alignment are always passed by reference.
+* All other aggregates follow the base calling convention.
+* Unions follow the same rules as aggregates: if they are `YLEN`-bit aligned and less than or equal to `2*YLEN` bits in size,   they are passed in memory layout in `YLEN` registers.
+  Otherwise, the base calling convention rules apply.
+
+==== Variadic and On-Stack Arguments
+
+In the pure-capability ABIs, variadic and on-stack arguments are handled differently from the base integer calling convention to ensure capability safety and allow for bounded `va_list` implementations.
+
+1. All variadic arguments (those corresponding to the `...` in the function prototype) are passed on the stack.
+They never occupy argument registers `a0`-`a7`.
+Each variadic argument is passed in a `YLEN`-aligned stack slot.
++
+NOTE: Passing all variadic arguments on the stack simplifies the implementation of `va_list` and ensures capability safety.
+Measurements on other architectures (AArch64) have shown that most variadic functions are simply wrappers around a function taking a `va_list`.
+In standard ABIs that pass variadic arguments in registers, the callee must spill these registers to the stack to create a contiguous `va_list` structure, which adds overhead and complicates the implementation.
+Passing all variadic arguments on the stack from the start simplifies these wrappers and avoids complex register-to-stack spilling logic.
+Using `YLEN`-sized slots for all arguments, including those smaller than `YLEN`, further avoids the need for complex logic to determine the offset of each argument.
+This approach has been used successfully in other CHERI-enabled architectures such as Morello and was also adopted by Apple in the variadic calling convention for AArch64 on iOS and macOS.
+
+2. A capability that covers all on-stack arguments on the stack is passed in the `x5` (`t0`) register.
+3. For variadic functions, this capability has its `Store` and `Execute` permissions cleared.
+4. If no on-stack arguments are passed to a variadic function, the `x5` register is set to null.
